patterns.title: New York and London banking axis
patterns.summary: The Federal Reserve Bank of New York is formally owned by its member banks: at end-2018 Citibank held 42.8% of its stock, JPMorgan Chase 29.5% and HSBC's US bank 6.1%, the last with its ultimate parent in London. In the 1920s the partnership of Benjamin Strong (New York Fed) and Montagu Norman (Bank of England, earlier a partner at the merchant bank Brown Shipley) set much of the direction of world finance; in 1925 the New York Fed opened a $200 million gold credit for the Bank of England and J.P. Morgan & Co. a $100 million credit for the British government so that sterling could return to gold. The London houses Morgan Grenfell (half-owned by J.P. Morgan & Co. from 1910) and Brown Shipley (a branch of Brown Brothers until 1914) were London ends of New York banks, and J.P. Morgan & Co. led the American banking group that took the US share of the Bank for International Settlements in 1930. Since 31 October 2013 the Fed and the Bank of England have had a standing swap line.

patterns.title: Basel and the central bankers' clubs
patterns.summary: The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) was set up in Basel in 1930 under the Young Plan to handle German reparations; its first capital came from five European central banks plus a Japanese banking group and an American group led by J.P. Morgan & Co., and its first president was Gates McGarrah, former chairman of the New York Fed. Under a 1987 agreement with Switzerland its premises and archives are inviolable, it is immune from Swiss courts and from seizure of its assets and of deposits placed with it, and it pays no Swiss taxes; it is audited by a private firm (PwC up to the year to March 2026), not by a national audit office. Around it sit the Basel Committee (1974), which writes the bank-capital rules its members commit to apply, the Financial Stability Board (1999/2009), the invitation-only Group of Thirty (1978), which seats serving central bankers beside private bankers, and the Kansas City Fed's Jackson Hole meeting (since 1982).

patterns.title: France's franc zone in Africa
patterns.summary: The CFA franc was created on 26 December 1945, the day France ratified Bretton Woods; its name first meant 'franc of the French Colonies of Africa'. The French Treasury guarantees unlimited convertibility at a fixed rate (now 1 euro = 655.957 CFA francs); in return the central banks kept operations accounts at the French Treasury and deposited part of their reserves there: the BEAC (Central Africa) at least 50% (65% before 2007) and the Comoros at least 65%, while the BCEAO (West Africa) deposited 50% until its account was closed in January 2020. France devalued the CFA franc by 50% on 12 January 1994 and paid the BCEAO about €40 million a year in interest on its deposits (2018-2019). Under the agreement of 21 December 2019 France left the West African bodies' boards, but it still guarantees the currency and the six Central African states and the Comoros remain under the old terms.

patterns.title: Banknote printers bribing central banks
patterns.summary: Banknote printers owned by central banks paid bribes to win note contracts from other central banks. Securency (50% owned by the Reserve Bank of Australia from 1996) and Note Printing Australia (an RBA branch, then RBA company from 1998) pleaded guilty in October 2011 to conspiring to bribe officials over notes for Indonesia, Malaysia, Vietnam and Nepal between 1999 and 2004, and gave up A$19.8 million and A$1.9 million in proceeds. In Vienna, managers of OeBS, a 99.75% subsidiary of Austria's central bank, were convicted of padding contracts for the central banks of Azerbaijan (20%) and Syria (14%) and routing the excess back to local decision makers. The private British printer De La Rue was investigated by the UK Serious Fraud Office over South Sudan (2019-2020); the case was closed without charges.

patterns.title: Wall Street and central bank revolving door
patterns.summary: Many central bank chiefs came from, or went to, the same few private firms. Goldman Sachs alumni include Mario Draghi (Goldman International vice chairman 2002-2005, then Bank of Italy and ECB), Mark Carney (13 years at Goldman, then Bank of Canada and Bank of England), William Dudley (Goldman chief US economist, then New York Fed), Neel Kashkari (Minneapolis Fed) and Hafize Gaye Erkan (Türkiye, 2023); Robert Kaplan went from Goldman partner to the Dallas Fed and back to Goldman as vice chairman in 2024. Fed chairs and vice chairs came from Carlyle (Powell, Quarles), Morgan Stanley (Warsh, chair from May 2026) and Citigroup (Stanley Fischer, before the Bank of Israel). Exits run to BlackRock (Hildebrand, Fischer), Citadel and PIMCO (Bernanke), Warburg Pincus (Geithner), UBS (Weber), Commerzbank (Weidmann), Brookfield (Carney) and Goldman (Corrigan).

patterns.title: Frozen and seized central bank reserves
patterns.summary: Central banks keep much of their reserves in New York, London and Brussels, which lets the US, UK and EU freeze them. The New York Fed held about 507,000 gold bars (6,331 tonnes) for governments and central banks in 2024 and $2.63 trillion of US Treasuries in custody for foreign official accounts in July 2026; the Bank of England holds about 400,000 bars and calls itself the second-largest gold custodian. The US froze Iran's central bank assets in 1979, more than $34 billion of Libyan government assets in 2011 and about $9.5 billion of Afghanistan's central bank in 2021; the Bank of England has withheld 31 tonnes of Venezuelan gold since 2019. After February 2022 Western states immobilised Russian central bank assets, about €185 billion of them at Euroclear in Brussels; the EU has sent their windfall profits to Ukraine since 2024 and in December 2025 froze them indefinitely and kept the right to use them to repay a €90 billion loan to Ukraine.

patterns.title: Fed swap club versus PBoC network
patterns.summary: Swap lines let a central bank borrow another's currency in a crisis, and the Fed decides who can borrow dollars. In 2007-2008 it opened lines with 14 central banks, with use peaking at $583 billion on 17 December 2008, but left out Russia, Turkey, India, Chile, Hungary and Iceland; on 31 October 2013 it made lines with only five (ECB, Bank of England, Bank of Japan, Bank of Canada, SNB) standing, and gave nine others temporary lines again in March 2020. The People's Bank of China has built a rival yuan network with 32 countries and regions (as of 30 September 2025); a 2023 study counted more than $170 billion of PBoC swap-line drawings in rescue operations for 22 countries from 2000 to 2021.

patterns.title: Gulf oil states pegged to the dollar
patterns.summary: Five of the six Gulf Cooperation Council states fix their currencies to the US dollar: Saudi Arabia at 3.75 riyals since 1986, the UAE at 3.6725 dirhams (official since 1997), Qatar at 3.64 riyals, Oman and Bahrain; Kuwait switched to a basket in May 2007. A US-Saudi Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation was set up at the same time to recycle petrodollars into US goods and services. The PBoC has since signed yuan swap lines with Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Qatar.

patterns.title: Global wave of central bank independence laws
patterns.summary: From 1989 country after country passed laws shielding central banks from governments. Chile (Law 18.840) and New Zealand (Reserve Bank Act) led in 1989; Garriga's dataset counts 343 country-year reforms raising independence from 1970 to 2023, 135 of them in 1989-1999, with peaks of 16-18 a year in 1991-1993 as post-socialist states wrote new laws and another in 1998 when euro members handed policy to the ECB. Studies tie the wave to outside pressure: reforms follow IMF loan programmes (Romelli 2022; Kern, Reinsberg and Rau-Göhring 2019, 124 countries 1980-2012), and EU treaty articles 130-131 require independence before euro entry. Since 2010 increases have slowed while reforms cutting independence continue (Garriga: 73 country-year decreases in all).

patterns.title: Waves of banking crises and rescues
patterns.summary: Systemic banking crises, which central banks and treasuries end with liquidity loans and bailouts, come in waves. The IMF's Laeven-Valencia database (1970-2025) shows clusters in 1980-1983 (Latin America's debt crisis: Argentina, Chile, Mexico, Uruguay, Colombia, Ecuador), 1994-1995 (Mexico and a run of transition and African economies, 24 starts), 1997-1998 (Asia and Russia, 15 starts) and 2007-2008 (the US and UK, then 22 more, mostly in Europe). Fiscal costs reached 55.1% of GDP in Argentina (1980), 56.8% in Indonesia (1997), 43.8% in Thailand and 37.6% in Iceland and Ireland (2008). The map's own corruption file holds 15 cases where central banks are accused of hiding losses or rescuing failing banks.

patterns.title: Governments removing central bank governors
patterns.summary: Alongside the laws protecting central banks, governments keep removing or pressuring their governors. Türkiye's president replaced four governors by decree between July 2019 and June 2023, usually after disputes over interest rates; Nigeria, Zambia, Malawi, Iran, Libya, Sudan and Myanmar's junta removed governors in 2020-2025, and governors in Ukraine (2020) and Bangladesh (2024) resigned under pressure. In the US, President Trump announced the firing of Fed Governor Lisa Cook in August 2025 and the Justice Department served the Fed with grand jury subpoenas in January 2026; the Supreme Court let Cook stay on the board in June 2026. The legal record shows the same drift: Garriga codes 73 country-year reforms that lowered independence from 1970 to 2023; since 2000 there were 3 or more a year in 2003-2004, 2008, 2011 and 2018-2019.

patterns.title: Lebanon's central bank financial engineering
patterns.summary: From 2015-2016 Banque du Liban (BdL) under Riad Salameh, governor for three decades until 2023, ran 'financial engineering': it gave commercial banks high returns to bring in dollar deposits from abroad and place them at the central bank, and paid premiums on government bonds. The Alvarez & Marsal forensic audit found BdL's foreign-currency position went from a $7.2 billion surplus at end-2015 to a $50.7 billion deficit at end-2020 with no loss shown on the balance sheet, Bank Audi and Blom Bank as the largest beneficiaries, and $111 million in commissions to unknown recipients; its 2018 accounts, signed with qualifications by EY and Deloitte, booked a $6.82 billion 'seigniorage' asset. Separately, about $330 million flowed in 2002-2015 through Forry Associates, a British Virgin Islands company owned by Salameh's brother, into property in France, Germany, Luxembourg and Belgium; the World Bank called the system 'Ponzi finance' in 2022 and the US, UK and Canada sanctioned Salameh in 2023.

patterns.title: City of London and its offshore islands
patterns.summary: London became the centre of offshore dollar banking in the late 1950s: after UK exchange controls of 1957 limited sterling lending to non-residents, London banks lent dollars instead, and Midland Bank bid for dollar deposits above the ceiling US rules (Regulation Q) allowed at home. The UK's overseas territories and Crown dependencies, which are not part of the UK but whose defence and foreign relations London handles, are among the largest secrecy jurisdictions: in the Tax Justice Network's 2025 Financial Secrecy Index the UK plus ten of them account for 9.26% of the global secrecy score, more than the United States alone (5.66%, rank 1). Two central bank cases in the map's files touch this network: Lebanon's Forry Associates was a British Virgin Islands company, and a Nigerian investigator said the CBN's former governor placed £543 million in UK fixed deposits without board approval.

patterns.title: Four firms auditing the central banks
patterns.summary: Most central banks that hire private auditors use one of four firms. Of 28 institutions whose auditor the map has traced (27 central banks plus the BIS), PwC, EY, KPMG and Deloitte audit 17: PwC signs for six central banks and the BIS, EY for five (including the Bank of England), KPMG for the US Federal Reserve Banks, Spain and Switzerland, and Deloitte for France (with Mazars) and Türkiye; seven others (Japan, Hong Kong, Singapore, Sweden, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand) are audited by state audit offices instead. The same firms also appear in scandals: EY and Deloitte qualified but signed Lebanon's 2018 central bank accounts that carried a $6.82 billion invented asset.
